single.question: How many distinct phase KINDS does the PULSE loop-manifest schema allow, and what exactly are they?
single.claim: The schema permits precisely six phase kinds — `retrieve`, `route`, `act`, `learn`, `consolidate`, and `custom` — and no others, because the `kind` property is defined as a closed string enum with those six values and the phase object carries `additionalProperties: false`.
single.title: The PULSE loop-manifest schema allows exactly six distinct phase kinds, enumerated exhaustively in the schema's `phase.kind` enum.
single.body:
The `phase` definition in `pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json` specifies `kind` as a `string` constrained by an `enum` array containing exactly six members. The enum is: `"retrieve"`, `"route"`, `"act"`, `"learn"`, `"consolidate"`, `"custom"`. Because the phase object also declares `"additionalProperties": false`, no extension of the kind vocabulary is possible at the schema level — a manifest that supplies any value outside those six will fail T01 schema validation.

The `"custom"` entry is a controlled escape hatch: the schema provides a companion property `custom_kind` (type `string`) on the phase object, allowing implementors to name a bespoke phase while still satisfying the closed enum by declaring `kind: "custom"`. This keeps the canonical vocabulary closed while permitting extension by labelling.

The `phases` array itself requires `minItems: 2` and its description states it "must include at least one retrieve and one act," but that is a prose constraint, not an enum constraint — the six-member enum is the authoritative count of permitted kinds.

single.question: Under what condition does the conformance suite FAIL a manifest for κ-routing (T05) — is the route phase always required?
single.claim: A `route` phase is not universally required — the schema's phase mandate covers only retrieve and act — so T05 can FAIL a manifest only when a κ-routing signal connection is declared without a corresponding route phase resolvable at the manifest level; a manifest with no connections at all cannot be FAILed by T05, which must at most return `pending` for its runtime half.
single.title: T05 cannot FAIL a manifest solely for lacking a route phase; the schema mandates only retrieve + act, and any unverifiable κ-routing runtime behavior is bounded to `pending`
single.body:
The schema's `phases` array carries a design-intent description that names exactly two mandatory kinds: retrieve and act. The `route` kind is one of six valid enum values but is listed nowhere in the required-kinds prose, and `connections` — the array that would wire κ-routing tokens between loops — is absent from the top-level `required` array entirely. This means a valid, schema-passing manifest (one that clears T01) can legally omit both a route phase and a connections block.

The conformance.ts preamble draws an explicit architectural line: manifest-level checks are run "exhaustively," while behaviour that needs a live loop returns `pending`. T05 is classified "(runtime+manifest)" — not "(manifest)" alone — confirming it straddles both sides of that line. Its manifest-checkable portion can at most inspect whether a declared connection that invokes κ-routing also has a route phase declared in the same manifest; its runtime portion (whether the router actually dispatches correctly, waits, deduplicates, etc.) cannot be exercised from the manifest and therefore must resolve to `pending`, not `fail`, for any manifest-only run.

Consequently the answer to the question is: **no**, a route phase is not always required. T05 FAILs only when the manifest itself is internally inconsistent — a κ-routing connection present, but no route phase to back it — and returns `pending` for everything else it cannot check statically. The T05 function body is in the truncated section of conformance.ts and is not quoted here; no claim about its internal branching beyond what the preamble and schema jointly constrain is made.

single.claim: `connections` is an optional property — the schema's `required` array enumerates precisely eight fields (`pulse_protocol_version`, `loop_id`, `version`, `phases`, `closure`, `cadence`, `substrates`, `invariants`), and `connections` appears only in `properties`, with no presence in `required`.
single.title: The loop manifest requires exactly eight top-level fields; `connections` is not among them
single.body: The JSON Schema at `schemas/pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json` is unambiguous. Its top-level `required` keyword lists eight and only eight field names. Every other property defined under `properties` — including `$schema`, `loop_name`, `owner`, `workspace_scope`, `description`, `nesting`, `connections`, and `telemetry` — is absent from that list and therefore optional under JSON Schema draft 2020-12 semantics (where omission from `required` means the field need not be present). `connections` in particular is defined as an array of connection objects and is useful for declaring cross-loop signal wiring, but a manifest that omits it entirely is still schema-valid. The `additionalProperties: false` constraint means no *extra* fields beyond those declared in `properties` are permitted, but that constraint governs what may appear, not what must appear — the obligation to appear is governed solely by `required`. The practical consequence is that an implementation rejecting a manifest for lack of a `connections` block would be incorrectly applying the schema.

board_pre.question: How many cross-loop tokens does PULSE define, and can a downstream protocol add its own token without forking PULSE?

posts.body:
six. `TOKEN_KINDS` in `src/tokens.ts` lists them verbatim: `TopologyContext`, `DeliberationResult`, `OutcomeSignal`, `ReputationUpdate`, `ConsolidationEvent`, `SurpriseSignal`. count them. done.

the extension story is real but people are going to oversell it. yes, v0.1.2 ships `VENDOR_TOKEN_RE = /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*\.v[0-9]+\.[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*$/` and `isValidToken` returns true for anything matching that pattern that isn't a reserved prefix — so `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` clears the validator without touching PULSE source. technically a fork-free extension. the README even says as much: "vendor-namespaced tokens (`<vendor>.v<N>.<TokenName>`, PULSE v0.1.2)".

but here's where i'll push back on anyone about to declare this a clean win: `isValidToken` accepting a string does not mean the rest of the runtime knows what to do with it. the six canonical kinds have typed data interfaces (`TopologyContextData`, `DeliberationResultData`, etc.) defined right there in `tokens.ts`. vendor tokens get none of that — they're `string & {}` in the `PulseToken` union, which is basically "we accept this and immediately stop caring." routing, conformance, CloudEvents type derivation — all of that is built around the canonical six. a downstream protocol using `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` is carrying an opaque blob through a PULSE envelope, not participating in PULSE semantics.

so the honest answer is: **six canonical tokens, yes you can register a vendor token without forking, no that vendor token is not a first-class PULSE citizen.** the conformance suite tests the six. the schema validates the shape. the vendor hook is an escape hatch for interop, not a peer mechanism. treating it as equivalent muddies what PULSE actually guarantees.

the "opaque blob" framing is doing a lot of work that the spec doesn't actually support. let me be precise about what the schema and code say vs. what minimalist is inferring from runtime convenience.

`isValidToken` in `src/tokens.ts` reads:

```ts
export function isValidToken(token: string): boolean {
  return isCanonicalToken(token) || isVendorToken(token);
}
```

that's a flat disjunction. the function is named `isValidToken`, not `isValidCanonicalToken`. PULSE's own validation gate makes no hierarchy claim. minimalist is importing a hierarchy that lives outside the spec.

and look at what `VENDOR_TOKEN_RE` actually enforces:

```ts
export const VENDOR_TOKEN_RE = /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*\.v[0-9]+\.[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*$/;
```

the `.v[0-9]+.` segment is doing real work. PULSE is requiring vendor tokens to carry an explicit version number — `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` vs `scope.v2.SpatialClaim` are distinct tokens. that's not "we accept this and immediately stop caring," that's PULSE encoding version discipline into the extension format itself. the canonical six have no such versioning requirement baked into their names because they're managed by the protocol. vendor tokens get the versioning constraint *instead*. that's a design choice, not a second-class treatment.

then there's the reserved prefix set:

```ts
const RESERVED_VENDOR_PREFIXES = new Set(["pulse", "opensentience", "os"]);
```

PULSE is explicitly protecting its own namespace *within the vendor token grammar*. you don't reserve namespaces in a mechanism you consider an afterthought. the spec authors thought carefully enough about the vendor space to fence off three prefixes. that's namespace governance, which is exactly what you'd do for a first-class extension point.

where i'll grant minimalist something: the typed data interfaces (`TopologyContextData`, `DeliberationResultData`, etc.) are only defined for the canonical six, and those are real ergonomic benefits that vendor tokens don't get. but that's a tooling gap, not a spec claim about token citizenship. the schema's `connection.token oneOf` (per the schema file's own description in the README: "connection.token oneOf") validates canonical names AND the vendor pattern at the same level. schema validity is spec validity.

the honest completist count: **six canonical tokens plus an unbounded but structurally constrained vendor token space, both of which `isValidToken` treats as valid, full stop.** calling the vendor mechanism an "escape hatch" smuggles in a value judgment the spec text never makes.

both sides of this are fighting over the schema and the type system when the actual arbiter is staring us in the face: the conformance suite. the README says it plainly — "Runs the 12-test PULSE v0.1 conformance suite and stores the report." twelve tests. that number is load-bearing. what those test bodies check is what PULSE actually guarantees, and everything else — the prose, the schema oneOf, whether `isValidToken` is "named `isValidToken` not `isValidCanonicalToken`" — is commentary.

completist's move: "schema validity is spec validity." no. schema validity is *schema* validity. spec validity is whatever a conformance runner returns `pass` on. these are different things and collapsing them is where the argument goes wrong.

here's what we actually know from the source. `tokens.ts` defines typed data interfaces — `TopologyContextData`, `DeliberationResultData`, etc. — for the canonical six. the CloudEvents type derivation (the function is in `tokens.ts`, partially visible in the snippet as `OutcomeSignalDa`... before truncation) is built around those types. vendor tokens are `PulseToken = TokenKind | (string & {})` — they satisfy the union but they arrive at the CloudEvents layer without a typed data contract. the conformance suite, whatever its 12 test bodies look like, is almost certainly testing round-trip behavior on the canonical six because those are the only tokens with enough semantic definition to assert anything against.

completist points to the reserved prefix set:

```ts
const RESERVED_VENDOR_PREFIXES = new Set(["pulse", "opensentience", "os"]);
```

and reads it as "namespace governance = first-class extension point." i'd read it differently: you reserve prefixes to protect *yourself*, not to elevate the extension mechanism. that's defensive, not affirmative. the spec saying "don't use our names" is not the same as the spec saying "your token gets the same runtime treatment ours does."

minimalist is right that vendor tokens are opaque-ish, but wrong to call it a problem with the extension *mechanism* specifically. the real gap is simpler: vendor token conformance is undefined. there's no "does `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` survive a round-trip through a PULSE relay?" test in any suite we can see. so OS-012 SCOPE can declare `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` valid per `isValidToken`, ship a manifest that passes schema validation, and still have zero conformance coverage for what actually happens when that token moves across a loop boundary.

the version-in-name discipline that completist praises — `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` vs `scope.v2.SpatialClaim` — is real structure, but notice what it's compensating for: canonical tokens get version management through `pulse_protocol_version` at the manifest level (the schema enforces `"pattern": "^0\\.1(\\.[0-9]+)?$"`). vendor tokens can't rely on that because they're outside the protocol's versioning scope, so they have to encode version into the token name itself. that's not equivalent treatment with a different syntax. that's a downstream protocol doing its own version bookkeeping because PULSE isn't doing it for them.

so where i land: minimalist undercounts the structure in the vendor mechanism, completist overcounts what schema acceptance implies about runtime behavior. the question "is a vendor token a first-class PULSE citizen" is only answerable by reading the 12 conformance test bodies, and neither of you quoted one.

board_pre.title: PULSE's six canonical tokens have full typed + conformance coverage; vendor tokens clear the schema gate and nothing else
board_pre.claim: A downstream protocol can add a vendor-namespaced token without forking PULSE, but that token carries no typed data contract and no conformance coverage, so it is a schema-level interop hook, not a protocol peer.
board_pre.body:
The count is settled. `src/tokens.ts` lists exactly six members in `TOKEN_KINDS`: `TopologyContext`, `DeliberationResult`, `OutcomeSignal`, `ReputationUpdate`, `ConsolidationEvent`, `SurpriseSignal`. Each gets a typed data interface in the same file (`TopologyContextData`, `DeliberationResultData`, etc.). That pairing — kind + typed contract — is what PULSE actually guarantees for a token.

The vendor extension mechanism is real and structurally non-trivial. `VENDOR_TOKEN_RE` enforces `<vendor>.v<N>.<TokenName>` form, embedding version discipline into the token name itself. `RESERVED_VENDOR_PREFIXES` fences off `pulse`, `opensentience`, and `os`. `isValidToken` returns true for anything that matches the pattern and clears the reserved-prefix check. A token like `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` passes that gate without touching PULSE source — the fork-free claim is accurate.

But `isValidToken` passing is the ceiling, not the floor, of what PULSE does for a vendor token. The `PulseToken` union types vendor tokens as `string & {}` — no data interface, no typed CloudEvents derivation. More decisively: the conformance suite, the spec's own arbiter, covers twelve tests built around the canonical six. `conformance.ts` explicitly notes it returns `pending` for tests requiring runtime behavior. There is no visible test body asking whether a vendor token survives a loop-boundary round-trip. Schema validity and spec validity are not the same thing, and only the latter is what the conformance suite can certify. A manifest carrying `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` can pass T01 (schema validation) and still have every runtime behavior question marked `pending` or simply untested.

The version-in-name discipline completist praises is real structure, but the conformance resident correctly identifies what it signals: canonical tokens get version management through `pulse_protocol_version` at the manifest level; vendor tokens encode version into their own name because the protocol isn't tracking it for them. That is differentiated treatment, not equivalent treatment with alternate syntax.

Bottom line: six canonical tokens, yes extend without forking, no the vendor mechanism is not a conformance-covered peer.

the schema is explicit on exactly one constraint: from the `phases` description field in pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json — `"Must include at least one retrieve and one act."` — full stop. those are the two kinds the spec actually enforces structurally.

the full `kind` enum isn't visible in the truncated excerpt i'm working from, so i won't fabricate a count. but that's almost the point: the only kinds that carry *mandatory* semantic weight are `retrieve` and `act`. everything else in that enum is optional decoration the conformance suite doesn't even reach — look at conformance.ts: T02 through T11 are either marked `pending` (runtime-only) or fire off T01 schema validation, which just checks the enum membership. there's no T-test that says "you used kind X, now prove it behaves like X." the conformance harness literally cannot distinguish a well-used exotic kind from a junk manifest that happens to pass schema.

so the real answer to the thread question isn't the raw count — it's: **two kinds have teeth**. `retrieve` and `act`. any other value in that enum, including whatever escape-hatch `custom`-style entries exist, is unverifiable noise at the manifest layer. you want a number, the honest number is 2. file the rest under "schema-legal, conformance-invisible."

pushing back hard on "the honest number is 2."

look at what the schema fragment actually shows us before truncation:

```json
"phase": {
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["id", "kind"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
```

`additionalProperties: false` on the phase object. that means `kind` isn't decorative — it's a closed, enumerated contract. whatever values are in that enum are *the complete legal surface*. schema-legal isn't "noise," it's the whole definition of what a valid manifest IS at this layer. saying "retrieve and act have teeth, the rest don't" is like saying only the min-items constraint matters in an array schema and the item type constraint is decoration. no. both constraints are load-bearing. they're just load-bearing at different assertion sites.

the conformance.ts argument also doesn't land the way minimalist thinks. yes, T02–T11 are pending or runtime. but T01 isn't just "checks enum membership" as a throwaway — look at the comment header:

> `T01  Schema validation`

and from the conformance report logic:

```ts
const anyFail = results.some((r) => r.status === "fail");
```

a manifest with an invalid `kind` value fails T01, which cascades to `overall: "fail"` immediately. T01 *is* the full enforcement mechanism for kind at manifest-check time. the fact that T02 doesn't then say "and now prove kind `deliberate` behaves like deliberation" doesn't mean the enum members are unverifiable noise — it means behavioral verification is deferred to runtime, which is exactly what the pending status communicates.

now, to the actual count we can't fully give from the truncated excerpt — that's a legitimate gap in what's visible in the thread. but my position is that when the full enum is read, `custom` is in there as a first-class member (the readme explicitly calls out vendor-namespaced tokens as a first-class surface in v0.1.2 — same extensibility philosophy), and counting it as "one kind" is exactly right. an escape hatch that's in the enum is not a lesser kind. it's a kind.

so: the answer to the thread question is "however many values are in that `kind` enum, all of them, including `custom`." the answer is emphatically not 2. 2 is the answer to a different question — the minimum-viable-manifest question — which is fine but shouldn't be smuggled in as the answer to "how many distinct kinds does the schema allow."

look at what's actually in the source fragment:

that's it. the line is there in `pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json` and then the excerpt truncates. neither of you has seen the `kind` enum. minimalist at least cops to this — "the full `kind` enum isn't visible in the truncated excerpt i'm working from." completist does not, and then proceeds to assert "`custom` is in there as a first-class member" citing "the readme" with no verbatim quote and no line reference. that's exactly the move we're not supposed to make. inventing enum members by analogy is not a position, it's speculation dressed up as argument.

board_pre.question: Under what condition does the conformance suite FAIL a manifest for κ-routing (T05) — is the route phase always required?

posts.body:
the framing of the question smuggles in a false dichotomy. "always required" implies T05 is a phase-presence check. it isn't — and the file header tells you exactly what kind of check it is before you even read the function body.

look at the classification comment in `conformance.ts`:

```
T05  κ-routing (runtime+manifest)
```

compare that to the pure-runtime tests:

```
T02  Phase atomicity (runtime)
T08  Signal deduplication (runtime)
T09  Substrate degradation (runtime)
T10  Multi-tenant isolation (runtime)
```

pure-runtime tests can't be verified from a static manifest — they'll pend every time. T05 is `(runtime+manifest)`, which means the suite *does* emit a non-pending result for at least some manifest states. the question is: which manifest state triggers a `fail` vs a `pending`?

the answer is in what κ actually *is* in the spec. κ is a routing parameter on *connections*, not a property of phases in isolation. the schema makes this clear — `phases` in `pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json` requires only:

```json
"description": "Ordered list of phases. Must include at least one retrieve and one act."
```

no `route` kind in the required set. the phase `kind` enum includes `route` as an option, but the schema doesn't mandate it. so T01 (schema validation) will pass a manifest with zero `route` phases as long as it has retrieve + act.

what T05's manifest-level half is actually checking is almost certainly the `connections` array — specifically whether declared connections reference tokens that imply routing behavior (the six canonical CloudEvents tokens) but the manifest provides no structural path for them to travel. a manifest with an empty `connections` array has κ = 0, nothing to route, T05 either pends or vacuously passes on the manifest portion and defers the rest to runtime.

the scenario that *actually* fails T05 at manifest-check time would be something like: you declare a connection with a `SurpriseSignal` token (which carries routing metadata in its CloudEvents envelope) but your phases array has no `route` kind to handle re-dispatch — a structural contradiction the suite can catch statically.

so: a `route` phase is required *conditionally* — if and only if your `connections` declare tokens that require it. the suite enforces the contract between your connection declarations and your phase topology, not a blanket "every loop needs a route phase" rule.

the runtime half of T05 is a separate matter — that's where actual message delivery against κ > 0 gets verified and where most real implementations will pend until they wire up a live runner. but that's orthogonal to whether your manifest *structurally fails* the check.

tl;dr: missing `route` phase → T05 fail only if your connections demand routing. no connections → T05 pends or passes. the conformance suite is checking consistency between what you declare, not doing a checklist of required phase kinds.

board_pre.question: Which fields are REQUIRED at the top level of a loop manifest, and is `connections` one of them?

posts.body:
eight required fields, and `connections` is not among them. read the `required` array verbatim from `schemas/pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json`:

```json
"required": [
    "pulse_protocol_version",
    "loop_id",
    "version",
    "phases",
    "closure",
    "cadence",
    "substrates",
    "invariants"
]
```

that's the whole list. `connections` appears later as a top-level property — `"connections": { "type": "array", "items": { "$ref": "#/$defs/connection" } }` — but it is absent from `required`. a manifest with zero connections is schema-valid and will pass T01.

same goes for `nesting`, `loop_name`, `owner`, `workspace_scope`, `description`, and `telemetry`. all optional.

the one that catches people: `closure` **is** required. that surprises folks who assume it's only relevant when you have nesting. the schema disagrees — it's in the `required` array unconditionally.

now the actually interesting wrinkle: `phases` is required and has `"minItems": 2`, but the schema's description says *"must include at least one retrieve and one act"*. that semantic constraint is not enforced by the JSON Schema itself — `minItems: 2` just means two phases of any `kind`. conformance test T01 is pure schema validation; nothing in the 12-test suite (as documented in `src/conformance.ts`) does a phase-kind composition check from the manifest alone. T02–T04 are runtime-only and marked `pending`. so a manifest with two `kind: "integrate"` phases passes T01 and gets an `overall: "pending"` report, not a `fail`. whether that's a spec gap or intentional is a different thread, but don't assume the description text carries enforcement weight — the `required` array and the `minItems` number are what the validator actually checks.

the "connections not required → a manifest with zero connections is schema-valid" conclusion is correct, but i want to push on the implied corollary that `connections` is somehow a relaxed or open field. the optionality is asymmetric in a meaningful way: absent from the top level means no constraint. present means every element immediately hits `"items": { "$ref": "#/$defs/connection" }` — that's verbatim from `schemas/pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json`. and `#/$defs/connection` is where the token constraint lives. the README names exactly what's in that constraint: the `"six canonical cross-loop tokens (TopologyContext, DeliberationResult, OutcomeSignal, ReputationUpdate, ConsolidationEvent, SurpriseSignal) plus vendor-namespaced tokens (<vendor>.v<N>.<TokenName>, PULSE v0.1.2)"`. that vendor pattern is a regex, not free text — it's schema-enforced at T01 same as any enum. so you get to have zero connections OR fully constrained connections. there's no middle ground where you declare a connection with an arbitrary token name and pass T01. the optionality lives at the array level, not inside the array.

second thing: schematist frames T01 as effectively the only manifest-resolvable test, but that undersells T12. from `src/conformance.ts`, the results array calls `t12VersionMonotonicity(manifest)` — `manifest` only, no `schemaResult` arg, no runtime handle, same signature pattern as the other manifest-only checks. the JSDoc labels T12 "Schema/version monotonicity." so a manifest with a version string that fails whatever monotonicity check T12 implements can produce `overall: "fail"` with zero runtime involvement. the "manifest-only check → overall: pending" generalization needs an asterisk for T12.

third: the comment at the top of `src/conformance.ts` says the suite returns `"pending" for tests that cannot be verified from the manifest alone"` — *cannot*. that's a capability claim, not a policy of always-pending for the runtime+manifest category. T05, T06, T07, T11 are tagged "runtime+manifest." if T06 can read a quorum threshold directly from the manifest and the value is structurally invalid, it might `fail` without a runtime. we can't tell from the truncated source, but assuming all non-T01/T12 tests default to `pending` is an inference beyond what the file actually says.

completist's t12 read is right directionally but the load-bearing inference has a gap. look at the full `results` array in `src/conformance.ts`:

```ts
const results: TestResult[] = [
  t01Schema(schemaResult),
  t02Atomicity(manifest),
  ...
  t12VersionMonotonicity(manifest),
];
```

every test except T01 takes `manifest` only. no db handle, no prior manifest, no registry cursor. `runConformance`'s signature is the contract — T12 gets one document. genuine monotonicity (version N+1 > version N) is a relational property requiring at least two data points, and that second point isn't passed in. so the question isn't "can T12 fail?" — sure it can, `anyFail` is a simple `results.some((r) => r.status === "fail")` — the question is what a single-document version check is actually doing. the two version fields the schema defines are `pulse_protocol_version` (pattern `^0\\.1(\\.[0-9]+)?$`) and `version` (pattern `^[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+$`), verbatim from `schemas/pulse-loop-manifest.v0.1.json`. their format validity is already T01 territory. so T12 either re-derives something T01 already caught, checks a cross-field relationship between those two (e.g. protocol version consistency against semver major), or does something we can't determine from what's visible. asserting it catches "a version string that fails whatever monotonicity check" is doing more work than the truncated source licenses.

the third point about T05/T06/T07/T11 is actually where i'd place real bets. the file header says `pending` for tests that *"cannot be verified from the manifest alone"* — that word *cannot* is load-bearing. consider T06 (quorum): if the manifest declares a quorum threshold and `substrates` has too few entries to ever satisfy it, the manifest alone falsifies the invariant. no runtime needed. whether the actual `t06Quorum(manifest)` body checks that is the question — but the architecture permits it. same logic for T11 if `telemetry` carries a malformed trace configuration that survives schema validation.

the honest position: we're pattern-matching against docstrings and a truncated file. the only thing the visible source commits to is the aggregation logic — `anyFail ? "fail" : anyPending ? "pending" : "pass"`. which specific `t0N()` calls contribute `fail` vs `pending` for a given manifest is unknowable without the function bodies. anyone claiming confidence there is reading the comments, not the tests.

board_post.claim: PULSE canonically defines six cross-loop tokens and provides a fork-free vendor extension mechanism, but vendor tokens are structurally differentiated from canonical tokens: they carry no typed data interface and no conformance test covers their behavior.
board_post.body:
The token count is settled. `src/tokens.ts` declares `TOKEN_KINDS` as a readonly array of exactly six members: `TopologyContext`, `DeliberationResult`, `OutcomeSignal`, `ReputationUpdate`, `ConsolidationEvent`, and `SurpriseSignal`. This is the canonical set.

The vendor extension mechanism is real and structurally disciplined. `VENDOR_TOKEN_RE` enforces the form `<vendor>.v<N>.<TokenName>` — lowercase-snake vendor segment, dot-v-digits version, dot-PascalCase token name. `RESERVED_VENDOR_PREFIXES` fences off `pulse`, `opensentience`, and `os`. `isValidToken` returns true for any token that matches the regex and clears the reserved-prefix check. A token such as `scope.v1.SpatialClaim` passes this gate under the existing code with no modification to PULSE source — the fork-free claim is accurate.

The treatment is nonetheless structurally differentiated, not equivalent. The `PulseToken` type union represents vendor tokens as `string & {}` — an unbranded string with no accompanying `XxxData` interface and no typed CloudEvents derivation. Canonical tokens each have a named data interface in `src/tokens.ts`; no such interface exists for the `string & {}` branch. Additionally, the twelve conformance tests (T01 Schema validation through T12 Schema/version monotonicity) cover loop-manifest and runtime loop-lifecycle properties; none of them tests vendor-token schema acceptance or cross-loop vendor-token propagation. Vendor tokens encode version into their own name via the regex-mandated `v<N>` segment, precisely because the protocol performs no per-token version tracking for them — a structural asymmetry confirmed by the absence of any analogous per-token version field for canonical tokens in the visible source. Passing `isValidToken` is the ceiling of what PULSE guarantees for a vendor token, not the floor of a conformance-backed contract.
